name: Weld-Abyssal
geological_features: Deep oceanic trenches exceeding 25 kilometers depth
Geothermal vent fields creating underwater hot springs
Frozen polar caps covering 15% of the surface
specific_features: Gravity wells of unknown origin in the deepest trenches
description: Weld-Abyssal is a cold oceanic world where dark waters meet gleaming ice caps under a pale, distant sun. The ocean surface is remarkably still in the temperate zones, its waters so clear that the seabed is visible to depths of several hundred meters, revealing forests of kelp-like flora that sway in slow submarine currents. The polar regions are locked in permanent ice, their frozen surfaces scored by pressure ridges that resemble the seams of welded metal plates.

The cold air carries a crystalline clarity that makes distant objects appear closer than they are, a disorienting effect for first-time visitors. Beneath the surface, the water temperature varies wildly with depth, creating shimmering thermoclines that refract light into prismatic displays. The silence above the water is matched by a rich acoustic environment below, where the flora produces a constant low-frequency hum as it photosynthesizes.

The deepest trenches harbor gravity anomalies that cause localized increases in gravitational pull, pulling objects and water downward with greater force than the planet's mass would suggest. These wells follow no pattern that matches geological models, and unmanned probes sent to investigate the deepest points have returned with damaged sensors and corrupted data. Some researchers believe the anomalies are remnants of an ancient gravitational weapon; others suggest they are natural features of a type not yet understood.

Weld-Abyssal's pharmaceutical potential is significant, as its cold-water flora produces antifreeze compounds with applications in cryogenic medicine. The gravity wells, while hazardous to navigation, represent a scientific mystery that attracts funding from multiple research foundations. The planet's remoteness and cold climate have kept it largely uninhabited, but a proposal to establish a permanent deep-ocean research station is currently seeking approval.
